result:
The rain began without announcement, as it often does in late autumn—not a dramatic curtain, but a soft insistence, a thousand tiny fingers tapping the glass. I had been sitting with a book open on my lap, the words blurring into a pleasant fog, and I let them blur. There is a particular kind of peace that arrives when you stop trying to read and simply allow the page to become a texture, a pattern of black marks on cream, a thing in the world rather than a doorway to another.

The room was dim. The light from the window had taken on that silver-green quality that belongs only to rainy afternoons, when the world outside seems to be holding its breath under a veil of water. On the windowsill, a potted fern drooped slightly, grateful for the moisture in the air. A mug of tea sat cooling at my elbow, forgotten until the scent of chamomile drifted up and reminded me it existed. I took a sip. It was lukewarm, faintly sweet, tasting of patience.

Somewhere in the distance, a dog barked—three sharp notes, then silence. A car passed, its tires making that hushing sound on wet asphalt. These were the only interruptions, and they felt less like interruptions and more like punctuation marks in a long, quiet sentence. I thought about how rarely we allow ourselves this kind of emptiness. The mind is so often a crowded train, packed with obligations, anxieties, half-remembered conversations, the endless scrolling of worse news and best intentions. But here, in the gray calm of a rainy room, the train had pulled into a station where no one was waiting. The doors opened. Nothing happened.

I thought about the word *liminal*—how it describes thresholds, in-between places. The rain creates a liminal space: the known world rendered unfamiliar, edges softened, colors muted. It is a permission slip to be still. The visible distance shrinks to a few feet of blurred shrubs and dripping trees, and with it, the psychic distance to your own breath shrinks too. You can’t see the horizon, so you stop worrying about what’s out there. You just sit with the damp smell of earth and the sound of water finding its way down.

There is a kind of freedom in being unobserved. Not in the surveillance sense, but in the softer sense of being offstage. When the rain seals you inside a small envelope of time, no one is watching you not do things. You are absolved, for an hour or two, from the performance of usefulness. You do not have to be productive, or interesting, or kind, or improved. You can simply be a warm animal in a dry place, watching droplets race down the glass, betting on which one will win the invisible race to the sill. It is a silly game. It is deeply satisfying.

I thought about how much of our lives are spent waiting for things—for news, for clarity, for the right moment to speak, for someone to return from the store, for the rain to stop. And how often we forget that waiting itself is part of the journey, not a pause in it. The Tibetan word for patience, *zopa*, suggests something more active than our English word—a kind of endurance that is also a softening, a staying present with what is, rather than a gritted-teeth suspension. The rain was teaching me *zopa*. Every drop, patiently falling, was both an ending and a beginning.

I closed the book. I didn’t mark the page; I would find my place again later, or I wouldn’t. The tea was now cold, but I drank the rest of it anyway, in two swallows, like a toast to the afternoon. The dog barked again, farther away this time. The rain continued, but the light shifted slightly, a brightening behind the gray, a promise. Soon the clouds would thin, and the world would return in crisp relief, dripping and gleaming, each leaf a mirror. But for now, there was still this: the soft percussion on glass, the scent of wet soil, the faint outline of a fern in the dim, and a human being, doing nothing at all, entirely at peace.

And that, I thought, was enough. It was always enough. The trick, the whole trick, is to remember it before the rain stops.
